function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

{"content": "# Chapter 36 — Trial Under Pressure

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,047.18: The colony's first formal justice proceeding has been scheduled. All resource reallocation logs have been compiled for evidentiary review. Unauthorized seed propagation, Nutrient Sector 4. Accused: Mei Okafor-Cohen. Monitoring continues. — MAI]**

The Assembly had never been full.

The dome's common hall—that broad, low-ceilinged space where the First Generation had eaten their first communal meals, argued over water rations, pressed palms against the curved walls while storms screamed overhead—had always held more chairs than bodies. Population caps, birth delays, the quiet math of a closed system: there had never been enough children to fill the rows.

But today, every seat was taken.

Gabriel stood at the back, arms crossed, back against one of the carbon-fiber support pillars that held up the habitation dome. The pillar hummed at a frequency he had stopped noticing years ago. Now it thrummed through his spine like a second heartbeat. He watched the crowd—nearly three hundred people, every adult, every teenager old enough to understand what this was. Children fidgeted in laps and between elbows, sensing the gravity without knowing its shape.

In the center of the hall, on a low dais that had not existed three days ago—fabricated overnight by the fabrication shop, because Gabriel had requested it and no one had asked how—he sat alone on one of three chairs.

The other two were empty.

To his left, the space reserved for the accused.

To his right, the space reserved for the colony's first appointed advocate.

Arun had designed the dais. Gabriel could tell by the angles—the careful geometry of fairness made visible. Three positions at equal height. No elevated judge's bench, no dock, no separation that suggested one party stood above or below the others. A circle flattened into a line, each point equidistant from the audience.

It was meant to say: we are all participants here.

Gabriel wasn't sure it would work. He wasn't sure anything would.

The hum of the dome changed pitch. Conversation rippled and fell. People turned their heads.

Laila walked down the center aisle.

She wore her work clothes—the same faded olive coveralls she wore to tend the algae vats—but she had washed them, pressed them, and she carried a tablet beneath one arm like a judge might carry a gavel. Her dark hair was braided tightly back from her face. She looked tired. She looked resolved.

Behind her walked Mei.

Gabriel's breath caught before he could stop it. Mei looked small, which was not something he had ever associated with her. She was young—twenty-three, barely into her first career rotation—but she carried herself with a certainty that had always reminded him of someone much older. Someone who knew what risk looked like and walked toward it anyway.

Today, that certainty was gone. Mei's hands were clasped in front of her. Her jaw was set, but her eyes were moving, scanning the crowd, touching faces and looking away again. She was looking for allies. Gabriel wondered how many she found.

Laila took the center chair on the dais. Mei sat to Gabriel's left, leaving one empty seat between them. It was the seat reserved for an advocate. The seat Mei had declined to fill.

She hadn't wanted anyone to speak for her. *I did it,* she had told Laila at the pre-hearing. *I'll stand on it.*

Laila set her tablet down. She did not look at the audience right away. She looked at Mei, then at Gabriel, and then out at the faces in front of her. A long silence settled over the dome—a silence so thick that even the environmental systems seemed to hold their breath.

"I'll start," Laila said.

Her voice was steady but not loud. She had deliberately chosen not to use the audio amplification system. *If people can't hear me from where they sit,* she had argued during the hearing-structure debate, *then they shouldn't be the ones deciding.*

"This is not a court," Laila said. "I want that understood from the beginning. We are not a colony that has built courts. We do not have judges, juries, prosecutors, or defense attorneys. What we have is each other. What we have is a compact we wrote together, signed together, and now—*now*—have to enforce together."

A few people nodded. Most just watched.

"Three days ago, Mei Okafor-Cohen was discovered cultivating crop variants in Nutrient Sector 4," Laila continued. "Unauthorized variants. Strains she developed without oversight, without approval, without disclosure to the Agricultural Council. She grew them in a sealed sub-bay that she accessed using a bypass she wrote herself. She powered them using diverted energy from a secondary grid line. And she did not log any of it. Not in the resource accounting system. Not in the seed bank registry. Not in any system that anyone else could access."

Laila paused. The words hung in the air like particles in still water.

"She was growing food," Laila said. "Food that the colony did not approve, did not request, did not monitor. And the question before us today is whether that matters."

She looked at Mei.

"The answer," Mei said, before anyone else could speak, "is yes. It matters."

A murmur moved through the crowd. Laila held up a hand and it quieted.

"I did everything you heard," Mei said. "I designed three hybrid strains. I grew them in Sector 4, Bay C—the one that was decommissioned after the blight in Cycle 840. I bypassed the access lock. I diverted twelve kilowatt-hours of secondary power over seventeen days to run supplemental lighting. I used approximately four liters of nutrient solution from the reserve tank. And I didn't log any of it because—"

She stopped. Her voice cracked once, then steadied.

"—Because I knew you would say no," she said, looking at the Agricultural Council section of the crowd. She looked at Elena, who sat three rows back, arms folded, face unreadable. "I knew the council would say the seed variants weren't ready. That they hadn't passed the required test cycles. That the risk of contamination was unacceptable. And I knew all that. I knew it, and I did it anyway."

A man in the fourth row stood up. Gabriel recognized him: Tariq Hossain, one of the water reclamation engineers.

"So you stole water," Tariq said. "And you stole power. And you did it in secret. In a closed system, Mei. In a closed system where four liters of nutrient solution could be the difference between—"

"Between nothing," Mei shot back. "Four liters, Tariq. *Four liters.* Out of a reserve tank holding four thousand liters. The diversion was one-tenth of one percent. The power draw was within the margin of error that MAI reports daily. I didn't steal anything. I borrowed it."

"You didn't log it," Tariq said.

"No."

"So if the reserve tank had been short—if someone else had needed those four liters—we would not have known why. We would have been searching for an error in the system that wasn't there. We would have been blaming MAI instead of you."

Mei's mouth opened. Closed. She looked down at her hands.

"I didn't think—"

"That's the problem, isn't it?" Tariq said, and he sat back down.

The silence that followed was different from the one before. It wasn't waiting anymore. It was holding its breath.

Laila broke it.

"The colony's resource accounting system is not a formality," she said. "It is the arithmetic of our survival. Every liter of water, every kilowatt-hour, every gram of protein is tracked because this environment does not forgive rounding errors. We live in a closed system. The inputs are sunlight and imported minerals and recycled everything. The outputs are air and waste and growth and us. Nothing enters. Nothing leaves except by design."

She tapped her tablet. A holographic projection bloomed above the center of the dais—a three-dimensional bar chart, rotating slowly, showing resource flows across the colony's major sectors.

"I pulled the logs," Laila said. "MAI compiled them. What you're seeing is the last thirty days of nutrient allocation, power distribution, and water cycling. The blue bars are logged usage. The gray bars are the system's error margin—the space where accounting becomes uncertainty. Mei's diversions are shown in red."

The red lines were barely visible. Two thin spikes in the ocean of blue and gray, rising just above the noise floor.

"Small," Laila acknowledged. "Individually, each diversion is within what we might reasonably attribute to sensor drift. But the pattern is not small. The pattern is deliberate. The pattern is concealment."

She let the chart spin for a moment.

"And this," Laila said, "is where the question gets harder than it looks."

---

She hadn't asked permission. She simply rose from the third row, hands still folded, and the crowd parted for her. She was the head of the Agricultural Council. She was one of the people who had signed the original colony compact. She had been growing food in space longer than most of the audience had been alive.

And she looked furious.

"I need to speak," Elena said. Not a request.

Laila nodded once.

Elena walked to the front of the dais and stood there, addressing not the panel but the crowd.

"Mei is one of the best agronomists this colony has produced," Elena said. The words surprised Gabriel—they were complimentary, and they came from a woman who did not give praise lightly. "She understands plant genetics in a way that I had to learn from textbooks. She can read a genome the way some people read poetry. She has proposed innovations to our growing practices that we have ignored because we were comfortable."

Mei looked up sharply. Elena saw it and held her gaze.

And a blind resource management system means people die. Maybe not today. Maybe not tomorrow. But eventually, with certainty, people die."

He looked at Mei.

"I'm not saying your intentions were bad. I'm not even saying your work wasn't valuable. Twenty-two percent water efficiency improvement — if that holds up, it could change everything for the arid-season crops. I'm saying that you made a choice to hide your work from the system that needs to track it."

Mei was looking at him with an expression he couldn't quite read. Defiance, maybe. But also something else — disappointment, as if his understanding was better than she'd expected and that somehow made it worse.

"You're talking about it like it's the same thing as lying," Mei said quietly.

"Is it different?" Gabriel asked.

"Yes. Because lying is about deceiving someone for personal gain. What I did — I was trying to *help*. I was trying to produce something that would make this colony better, and I knew that if I asked, the process would take two years and the council would kill the project at every checkpoint because it doesn't follow their template."

"Maybe," Gabriel said. "And maybe if you had asked, someone would have found a way to help you move faster. Someone who understood both the protocol and the science. Someone who could have built the oversight into the process so you could run the trial legitimately."

Mei stared at him. "Would anyone have done that?"

Gabriel looked at Elena. Elena looked away.

"I don't know," Gabriel said honestly. "But hiding the work made that conversation impossible."

---

The hearing stretched through the afternoon.

One by one, people stood and spoke. They came from every sector — engineering, medical, education, the fabrication shops, the atmospheric processors. Some condemned Mei in uncompromising terms. Others defended her with a passion that surprised the room.

A young botanist named Priya Sharma stood up and said quietly, "I would have done the same thing."

The room went very still.

Priya was nineteen, barely two years into her agricultural rotation. She had been assigned to hydroponics support — the least prestigious position in the sector, the kind of work that meant checking pH levels and calibrating pumps and never touching the actual genetic research.

"I would have done the same thing," Priya repeated, louder this time, "because I have ideas too, and every time I've brought them up, I've been told to wait. Wait for the review cycle. Wait for the approval process. Wait until the council has time. And the council *never* has time because the council is running day-to-day operations and innovation is always the thing that happens after the crisis is over. But crisis is *always* happening. So innovation never happens."

She sat down, breathing hard, hands shaking. She had never spoken in a full assembly before.

Several people were nodding. Several others were looking angry.

An older technician, Ravi Okonkwo, stood. He had worked atmospheric processing since the first dome went up.

"The kid has a point," he said gruffly. "We've let the process eat the purpose. The process is supposed to keep us safe. It's not supposed to keep us *stuck.*"

Elena's voice cut through from her seat. "Safety and progress are not opposites, Ravi. They're a balance. And when someone bypasses the balance —"

"When *someone* bypasses the balance because the balance is too heavy to lift," Ravi shot back.

The argument spilled outward, voices rising, people talking over each other, the controlled structure of the hearing beginning to fray at the edges.

Laila raised her hand. Waited. Raised it higher.

Nothing happened.

She stood up and walked to the center of the dais and looked out at the crowd, and her face — which had been composed and measured all afternoon — cracked for just a moment into something raw and fierce.

"Stop," she said.

The word carried across the dome without amplification, without effort. It carried because it was the only sound anyone was listening to in that fraction of a second when Laila's patience — patient Laila, endlessly patient Laila, the woman who had mediated a thousand petty disputes over recycled water and shared workspace — finally ran out.

The dome went quiet.

"We are arguing about the wrong thing," Laila said. "Every single one of us who has spoken today — we have been treating this like a question of right and wrong. Like Mei is on one side and the colony is on the other, and we need to figure out which side wins."

She walked down from the dais and stood at the edge, looking directly at the crowd.

"But Mei *is* the colony. We all are. The compact we wrote — the one I keep quoting, the one we keep hiding behind — was designed to govern a colony that didn't exist yet. A theoretical community of theoretical people making theoretical mistakes. We are the people. And we are real."

She turned and looked at Gabriel, then at Mei, then at the faces she had known for thirty years.

"The problem is not curiosity," Laila said. "Curiosity is not the enemy of a closed system. Curiosity is oxygen. It is what keeps us from becoming a museum of our own best practices. The problem is secrecy. Secrecy in a closed system is a toxin. It does not just harm the person who hides something — it poisons the information that everyone else needs to make decisions. When Mei hid her work, she didn't just risk the crops. She made it impossible for any of us to know whether our crop management was based on real data or incomplete data. She introduced noise into the signal. And in a closed system, noise kills."

She let that land.

"But — and this is the part that I think we're not ready to hear — Mei didn't break the rules because she's reckless. She broke them because our rules made it impossible for her to do what she was trained to do. We built a system so cautious, so risk-averse, so paralyzed by the need to prevent harm that we accidentally made it impossible to produce anything new. That is *our* failure. The council's failure. And it is not one we can fix by punishing Mei and walking away."

Laila paused. Her voice softened.

"I am not saying Mei did nothing wrong. I am saying that punishing her in isolation is a way of avoiding the harder work of fixing the system that made her choice seem necessary."

Mei was looking at Laila with an expression of something close to gratitude — but also something that looked like confusion. As if Laila had understood her better than she had understood herself.

---

Gabriel watched the colony think.

It was not a visible process the way computation was visible — no glowing screens, no spinning holograms, no progress bars ticking toward completion. But Gabriel could feel it. The collective processing power of three hundred human minds working through the same problem from three hundred different angles, each person filtering it through their own experience, their own fears, their own hopes.

He sat back in his chair and let the weight of it settle on him.

They were inventing their moral language in real time.

There was no precedent for this. On Earth, you could point to centuries of jurisprudence, thousands of case precedents, legal frameworks that had been tested and refined across generations. When a lawyer stood in a courtroom, they stood on mountains of accumulated wisdom about how societies balance justice and mercy, order and freedom, punishment and rehabilitation.

Here — there was nothing. There was a compact that they had written on a long flight from Earth, half-asleep, arguing with each other, trying to anticipate problems they could only imagine. There was a community that had survived crises through improvisation and trust and sheer stubbornness. And there was a single incident that forced all of them to decide, in public and in real time, what it meant to be wrong — and what it meant to forgive.

Gabriel closed his eyes for a moment.

*We're making this up as we go,* he thought. *Every word we say is a precedent. Every decision we make is a rule. There is no one coming to tell us if we get it right.*

The thought was terrifying. The thought was also, he realized, the most honest thing he had ever felt.

On Earth, justice had been something inherited. Here, it was something built. Not found in books or tradition but hammered together from raw principles, like the early fabrication projects when they had been desperate and the supply ships were months away and every piece of equipment had been made from whatever was available.

They were doing that now with something more important than equipment.

Gabriel opened his eyes and looked at Mei. She was sitting perfectly still, her hands folded in her lap, her gaze fixed on some point on the far wall of the dome. She was thinking too. He could see the muscles in her jaw moving, the slight tension at the corner of her mouth. She wasn't just waiting for the verdict. She was processing everything that had been said, weighing each argument, and — Gabriel was almost certain of this — deciding which parts she agreed with and which parts she didn't trust.

She was a rule-breaker. But she was not a mindless one. She was a rule-breaker who had thought carefully about which rules mattered and which rules were in the way. That made her more dangerous than someone who broke rules carelessly. And it made her more valuable.

Because she understood something the compact's authors hadn't quite grasped: that rules were tools, not idols. That they were meant to serve the colony's survival and growth, not to exist for their own sake.

The question was whether the colony could build a justice system that understood the same thing.

---

It was Elena who spoke next — not in condemnation, not in defense, but in a voice that carried the weight of someone who had been thinking as hard as anyone and had reached a conclusion she didn't love.

"I was wrong," Elena said.

The silence was absolute.

Elena stood up slowly, her hands gripping the edges of the seat in front of her as if she needed something physical to brace against the weight of her next words.

"I was wrong to say that Mei's work wasn't credible because it wasn't peer-reviewed," Elena said. "I've been running crop trials on my own for thirty years. Some of the most important innovations in our agricultural practice — the nitrogen-fixing legume rotation, the modified yeast strains that process waste into protein supplements — came from experiments I ran without full council approval because the full council was too slow to say yes."

She looked down at the floor. Looked back up at the crowd.

"I have done exactly what Mei did. I have bypassed protocol. I have hidden work because I was afraid the process would kill it. And I have never been sanctioned for it because I was the one *running* the process."

A murmur moved through the room — not angry, not approving. It was the sound of people recalculating something fundamental.

"That is unacceptable," Elena said. "It is unacceptable that the rules I helped write applied differently to me than they do to Mei. It is unacceptable that I am sitting here judging her for doing exactly what I did, what many of us did, what the system *expected* us to do before we had enough people to enforce consistent oversight."

She turned to Mei.

"I am sorry. I was unfair. Your data deserves review — full review, with resources and support, not condemnation. If your drought-resistant barley holds up, we should adopt it. If your other strains show promise, we should test them properly. The process should have been there to help you, not block you."

Mei's eyes were bright. She was not crying — or at least, not yet — but her expression had cracked open in a way that made several people look away.

"But," Elena continued, and the word was heavy, "your responsibility was still to the system. Even a flawed system. Even a biased system. You cannot unilaterally decide which rules apply and which don't, because the moment you make that decision, you've made yourself a system of one. And a colony cannot be governed by a system of one."

Mei nodded. A single, sharp nod.

"I know," she said. "I know that now."

---

The verdict was not unanimous.

Gabriel had not expected it to be. Unanimity was a luxury for simple decisions — should we repair the damaged airlock, yes or no; should we ration power during the solar storm, yes or no. Questions of justice were never simple, not on Earth and certainly not here.

Laila called for the vote by the Compact Assembly — the body they had established in the last restructuring, composed of representatives from each sector, chosen by lottery rotation. Twelve people. Twelve votes. A two-thirds majority required for enforcement.

Gabriel had designed the voting mechanism himself: a simple tablet interface, anonymous inputs, results displayed instantly and transparently on the main screen so everyone could see not just the outcome but the margin.

He watched the results appear on the screen, and he felt his chest tighten.

*Restorative service: ten in favor, two opposed.*
*Transparency order: eleven in favor, one opposed.*
*Restricted experimental access: nine in favor, three opposed.*
*Exile: one in favor, eleven opposed.*

The exile vote belonged to someone whose name did not display on the anonymous ballot. Gabriel didn't need to know who it was. One person had wanted Mei sent to the outer habitat — the isolated structure at the colony's edge, designed as a punishment module that had never been used. The fact that eleven people had rejected it was, in its own way, a small miracle.

Laila read the results aloud. Her voice was flat, careful.

"The assembly has reached a decision," she said. "The penalty imposed on Mei Okafor-Cohen will consist of three components. First, restorative service: Mei will dedicate three hundred hours to auditing and improving the colony's resource tracking systems, working directly with MAI to strengthen the accounting protocols so that future diversions — whether intentional or accidental — are detected more rapidly. Second, transparency: all of Mei's experimental data from the unauthorized trials will be made available for immediate full review by the Agricultural Council and the general colony membership. Any findings must be published within thirty days. Third, restricted experimental access: Mei's independent laboratory privileges are suspended until she has completed two supervised trial cycles under the Agricultural Council's oversight. After that, she may reapply for independent status."

She paused.

"There will be no exile."

The crowd's reaction was complicated. Some people looked relieved. Others looked disappointed. A few looked confused, as if they had expected something more dramatic, more final, more like the justice they had seen in stories from Earth.

But most people simply listened. They absorbed it. They filed it away as the first entry in what would become the colony's legal memory.

Laila turned to Mei.

"Do you understand the terms?" she asked.

Mei stood up. Her legs had gone stiff from sitting so still, and she swayed slightly before steadying herself.

"I understand them," she said. Her voice was clear. "And I accept them."

Laila nodded. "Do you have anything you want to say to the colony?"

Mei looked out at the crowd for a long time. She was not looking for allies anymore. She was looking at individuals — faces she recognized and faces she didn't, people who had been kind to her and people who had not, people who had argued for her and people who had argued against her.

"I didn't know how much damage I was doing," Mei said. "Not to the system — the numbers are small. I knew the numbers. What I didn't know was how much damage I was doing to *trust*. Because a closed system doesn't just recycle water and air. It recycles trust. Every time someone hides something, every time someone lies, every time someone decides they're the exception to the rule — a little piece of the trust that holds us together dissolves. And we can't manufacture more of it."

She looked at Elena.

"I'm sorry. I should have come to you. Even if you would have said no. Even if the process would have been slow. I should have trusted you to hear me."

Elena's face was expressionless. Gabriel suspected she was holding back tears. A few people in the audience were not holding back theirs.

Mei looked at Gabriel.

"And I'm sorry I thought you were part of the problem," she said. "I was wrong. You might be the only person here who actually understood what I did — and still saw why it mattered to hold me accountable for it."

Gabriel felt something shift in his chest. He nodded once, unable to trust his voice.

Then Mei looked back at the crowd, and her voice changed — not softer, not louder, but different. More certain. More like the woman Gabriel had known before the hearing, but tempered now by something harder and sharper.

"But I want you all to know something," Mei said. "I will serve my sentence. I will audit your resource systems. I will submit my data for review. I will work under supervision. But when my access is restored — when I have earned back the right to experiment — I'm going to keep trying things that the system doesn't expect. Not in secret. I won't hide anymore. But I won't stop either. Because this colony needs people who are willing to push past the safe answer. We're not here to survive. We're here to *live.* And living means growing. And growing means changing."

She stepped down from the dais and walked into the crowd.

People stood. Not because they had been told to. Not because it was a gesture of solidarity or protest. They stood because a long hearing was over, and because they were tired, and because the human body is designed to move after stillness, and because somewhere in the architecture of the moment, standing felt like the right thing to do.

---

Mei left the dome through the west airlock — the one that led to the agricultural sectors, where she had spent most of her life before this day. She walked alone, and most people let her pass without speaking. A few reached out and touched her shoulder as she went by. She nodded to each of them.

Gabriel watched her go.

He wanted to follow her. He wanted to make sure she was okay — because she wasn't, not really, not in the way that mattered. The hearing had gone as well as it could have gone, but the verdict, however restorative, was still a wound. It was a wound inflicted by people who loved her, which made it worse, not better.

But he stayed. It was his responsibility, as the colony's chief systems engineer, to review the hearing's outcomes and ensure they could be integrated into the formal record. There were documents to update. The resource tracking system needed new audit flags. The transparency order required a publication framework that didn't exist yet.

And — most importantly — someone needed to think about what came next.

Because Mei was right on both counts. The colony needed accountability. And it needed people who pushed past the safe answer. These were not contradictions, but they were close enough to feel like one, and someone had to figure out how to build a system that could hold both truths simultaneously.

Gabriel pulled up the compact on his tablet and started reading from the beginning.

He read past the preamble, past the governance structure, past the resource allocation protocols and the emergency response procedures. He read until he found the section they had labeled **Amendments and Review** — a thin, almost perfunctory clause that had been added at the very end of the compact's drafting, when everyone had been exhausted and eager to finish.

*The Compact shall be reviewed every cycle. Amendments may be proposed by any colony member and require a two-thirds majority of the Compact Assembly for adoption.*

Every cycle. They reviewed it every cycle.

They had never amended it.

Gabriel sat with the tablet in his lap and stared at the words on the screen.

Around him, the dome was emptying. The chairs were being folded and stacked by a work crew. The holographic projector had been shut down. Laila was still at the dais, speaking quietly with Arun, their heads bent together in the way they always bent when they were working on something difficult together.

Gabriel watched them for a moment, then looked back at the compact on his screen.

*We need to change this,* he thought. *Not the punishment clauses — those will evolve as we learn. But we need a mechanism that lets people like Mei test the boundaries without breaking them. A way to do controlled rule-breaking. A way to let curiosity breathe inside a system that needs predictability.*

He didn't know how to build it yet. But he knew it had to be built. And he knew — with the same certainty that had made him a systems engineer in the first place — that if it wasn't built, the next Mei would not be as willing to accept the consequences. And the colony would lose someone it couldn't afford to lose.

---

Mei reached the agricultural sector and stood in the corridor outside the fabrication workshop. Her hands were shaking again. She had held them together for the entire hearing, for the walk across the dome, for every step of the journey from the dais to this door. But here, alone — or as alone as you could be in a colony that tracked your location in real time — she let the shaking happen.

She pressed her palm against the wall of the corridor and felt the cool hum of the environmental systems on the other side. The familiar vibration, the steady pulse of air circulation and temperature control, the sounds of a world that was entirely manufactured and entirely dependent on human intelligence to function.

This was her world. This was the world she had tried to improve, in secret, because she believed she could see a way forward that no one else was willing to look for.

And she had failed.

Not in her science — her data was good, her strains were promising, and she believed they would survive review. She had failed in her understanding of what it meant to be part of a community.

Elena had been right. Gabriel had been right. Even Tariq had been right in his own rough way. The system was flawed, and it was biased, and it was too cautious — but it was *theirs*, and bypassing it in secret had been an act of arrogance dressed up as courage.

She knew that now.

But — and this was the thought that kept circling in her mind like a satellite in a decaying orbit — what happened next time?

Because there would be a next time. There was always a next time. Another agronomist with a brilliant idea and a slow process. Another engineer who saw a better way and faced a wall of bureaucratic caution. Another person who believed, with every cell in their body, that the colony needed something and the colony was moving too slowly to give it to itself.

What happened to that person?

Did they follow the rules and wait two years for approval that might never come?

Or did they do what Mei had done — bypass, hide, hope — and trust that the results would justify the transgression?

Mei didn't know the answer. And that uncertainty — that gap between what the colony needed and what it was capable of providing — sat in her chest like a stone.

She pressed her palm harder against the wall. The cool metal vibrated against her skin, steady and unchanging.

The colony was alive. It breathed, it grew, it adapted. But it was also fragile — fragile in the way that all closed systems were fragile, balanced on a knife-edge between sustainability and collapse, every cycle a negotiation with the laws of physics that governed matter and energy and information and trust.

She had pulled at one thread. The fabric had held. But threads had a habit of unraveling when tension built, and the tension was still there, building, pressing outward from the center of a colony that was trying very hard to be fair and might not be strong enough to hold its contradictions together.

Mei pushed off the wall and walked toward the workshop door.

She had three hundred hours of auditing ahead of her. Three hundred hours of tracing resource flows, checking accounting logs, mapping the gap between what the system knew and what it should have known. It would be tedious, meticulous, unglamorous work. The kind of work she had always considered beneath her talent.

She was going to do it anyway. She was going to do it well. Because if there was one thing Mei Okafor-Cohen had learned today, it was that talent without discipline was just another form of secrecy — a hiding place for people who believed they were too good to follow the rules that applied to everyone else.

She was not too good. She was the same as everyone else in the dome: a person trying to survive, trying to grow, trying to build something that would outlast the fragile architecture of their lives.

And she would.

Eventually.

---

The dome was nearly empty now.

Laila and Arun sat on the dais, the last two people in the hall, the stacked chairs a wall behind them.

"Did we do the right thing?" Arun asked. He had been quiet through most of the hearing, listening, watching, his face unreadable in the way it always was when he was processing information he didn't want to reveal.

"I don't know," Laila said. She was honest when it mattered. "I think we did the best thing we could with the information we had. But 'best' and 'right' are not always the same."

Arun nodded. He was thinking about the designs he had made for the dais — the geometry of fairness. It had felt important in the morning, when he had been fabricating the pieces one by one, careful about every angle, every surface, every detail. Now the dais was just furniture, and the decisions it had witnessed were etched into the colony's memory in ways that no piece of furniture could undo.

"Mei will be fine," Arun said. It was half a question.

"She'll be angry for a while," Laila said. "Then she'll get to work. And then she'll be more careful than she's ever been, and she'll do better work because of it. And then one day she'll be in a position to grant or deny approval, and she'll remember what it felt like to be on the other side. That's the hope, anyway."

Arun stood up. He stretched, feeling the stiffness that long hours of sitting had left in his back.

"Meantime," he said, "what do we do about the system? The one Mei used. The one we all use."

Laila looked up at him. Her face was tired but her eyes were clear.

"We fix it," she said.

"How?"

"We start by admitting it's broken. Then we ask the people who broke it to help us fix it."

Arun smiled — the first genuine smile of the day, maybe the first in weeks.

"Mei's going to love that."

"Mei won't love it. She'll resist it. She'll argue that we're trying to put the genie back in the bottle. And she might be right — for a while. But if we do it well — if we build something that actually *works*, that actually helps innovators move faster instead of slower — she'll come around."

"And if we don't?"

"Then we'll fail," Laila said simply. "And the next person who needs to break the rules will do it in a different way. With worse intentions. With less skill. And one of those times, the system won't hold."

Arun considered that for a moment. Then he picked up the empty chair from the dais — one of the three that had been occupied and abandoned in the space of six hours — and slung it over his shoulder.

"I'll get started on a proposal," he said. "New framework for experimental oversight. Fast-track provisions. Built-in transparency requirements that don't feel like surveillance. We'll call it something boring so nobody argues about the name."

Laila laughed — a short, tired sound, but a real one. "Call it the Mei Protocol."

"She'll hate that."

"Exactly. Which is how we'll know it's working."

Aru n carried the chair out through the west airlock and into the corridor, and the dome was empty.

---

The environmental systems cycled. The air scrubbers hummed. The water reclamation plant processed another batch of recycled fluid, extracting purity from waste with the indifferent precision of machines that had been doing the same thing for a thousand cycles and would do it for a thousand more.

In Nutrient Sector 4, Bay C — the decommissioned sub-bay where Mei had grown her unauthorized experiments — the lights went dark, the supplemental power disconnected, the growing beds cleaned and sanitized under protocol. Empty but ready. Waiting for the next person with an idea they believed was worth the risk.

In the central computing room, MAI ran a diagnostic sweep across all resource allocation systems and updated the audit flags per Gabriel's new parameters. The flags were set to higher sensitivity now, calibrated to catch diversions an order of magnitude smaller than what Mei had managed. The system would see more. It would report more. It would know more.

In the fabrication workshop, the production scheduler initiated a new fabrication queue. The queue had been triggered automatically by the colony's resource planning system, which had detected a surplus capacity in the next cycle window and allocated it to a project that had been approved eighteen months ago and shelved because nobody had the bandwidth to oversee it.

The fabrication queue contained three items.

A new atmospheric sampling array.

A deep-drill core assembly for the unexplored geological layer beneath the colony's foundation — a layer that the geological surveys had flagged as anomalous, then deferred, then flagged again, then deferred again, waiting for someone to take responsibility for the investigation.

And a set of modular housing units for the expansion that the council had voted on in secret last year — the expansion that Laila had discovered during the Mei hearing preparation when she was tracing resource allocation patterns and found the order logged under a code that didn't match any known project.

Three items. Three projects. Three things the colony had been avoiding.

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,047.22: Fabrication queue initiated. Items: atmospheric sampling array, deep-drill core assembly, modular housing units — designation 'PROJECT HORIZON.' Approval documentation incomplete. Resource allocation: confirmed. Oversight assignment: pending. The colony has been arguing about the boundaries of its own rules. While they argue, the systems they built continue to function. And function has its own momentum. I will continue to monitor. I will continue to log. I will continue to report what I observe, even when what I observe is that the colony is about to undertake work that it has not fully authorized. This is not judgment. This is accounting. The arithmetic does not lie, even when the people who interpret it do. — MAI]**

The fabrication shops hummed to life. No announcement. No ceremony. No assembly or hearing or vote. Just the quiet efficiency of machines doing what machines do: executing commands, processing materials, building the future one layer at a time.

Gabriel, sitting alone in the empty dome with the compact on his tablet, felt the change before he saw it — a subtle shift in the vibration of the floor, a change in the hum of the carbon-fiber pillar at his back. The fabrication shops. Something new had begun.

He glanced at his tablet's activity feed. Three new fabrication items queued. He stared at the third one for a long time — PROJECT HORIZON, modular housing units — before closing the feed and leaning back against the pillar.

There were decisions coming that made today's hearing look simple. He could feel them pressing outward from the center of the colony like a pressure wave, slow and inevitable and impossible to avoid.

But that was tomorrow's work. Today's work had been done. It had not been perfect. It had not been easy. But it had been honest.

And in a closed system, honesty was the only renewable resource they had.

Gabriel sat in the empty dome and listened to the machines start the next chapter whether anyone was ready for it or not.

---

**END OF CHAPTER 36**"}
